promptHead: Athlete goal: 5K (Corrowmore Harvest 5K) on Sun Nov 15 2026, 10 weeks out, target run the whole way.

new.headline: Keep to three runs a week and add run time slowly, because running every day would add strain faster than your legs can adapt. This week adds about 12 percent more running time, all kept easy, with four relaxed strides on Wednesday.

flags.title: Calf tightness
flags.detail: the calves feel tight the day after runs and ease by morning, so keep the rest days. If the tightness turns into pain that lasts, grows across runs, or changes how you walk or run, see a physio or doctor before running again.

flags.title: Extra run days
flags.detail: three run days a week is enough for now, so hold off on the every-day idea until the 5K distance feels routine.

flags.title: Easy heart rate ceiling
flags.detail: keep heart rate under 145 bpm on every run; last week averaged 132 to 134 bpm, so there is room, but no reason to push.

flags.title: Walk breaks
flags.detail: cut them back gradually once a run-walk session feels comfortable; there are no pace targets yet.

answers.question: I want to be ready for the 5K in November. Should I run every day next week to get there faster?
answers.answer: No, running every day next week would not get you there faster. Three runs a week with rest days between is the right load for now, and the gains come from adding run time to each session. Extra days are the most common way new runners pick up strain and then lose weeks of training.

new.analysis:
The week of Aug 24 – 30 was a sound start: three runs, all easy, and pain at 0 out of 10 throughout. Your heart rate averaged 132 to 134 bpm, about 72 to 74 percent of your maximum, which is comfortably easy for where you are now.

Next week keeps the same three run days and adds only a little time to each run. The table shows the change.

| Measure | Aug 24 – 30 | Aug 31 – Sep 6 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Runs | 3 | 3 |
| Total running time | 64 min | 72 min |
| Longest run | 24 min | 26 min |

That is roughly 12 percent more total time, which is the kind of gradual growth a first block of running can absorb. The longest run grows by two minutes, so the step up stays small.

The phase is build, which normally adds threshold work. That is not right yet, because you have one week of running behind you. Strides are short, relaxed, and teach a quicker, lighter stride without building fatigue, so they fit this stage better.

Your calves feel tight the day after each run and ease by the next morning. That is a reason to keep the rest days between runs, not a reason to stop. It is also why the extra days you asked about would add load before the legs have caught up.

Over the coming weeks, the aim is to shorten the walk breaks as each run starts to feel comfortable, rather than adding days. A lighter week about every third week will let the body absorb the work. With ten weeks to go, there is enough time to run the full 5K if the walk breaks come out steadily and the calves keep settling.
